title: Review: Populations and communities; Transfers of energy and matter
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for IB Diploma Biology (review status in the bank: ai-specialist-reviewed-gate-verified-2026-09-21-awaiting-human-signoff). Clues: C4.2#c03 first sentence of the bank's definition; C4.2#c06 first sentence of the bank's definition; C4.2#c27 first sentence of the bank's definition; C4.2#c37 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: C4.1#q12, C4.1#q30, C4.1#q17, C4.1#q18, C4.1#q28, C4.1#q27, C4.2#q01, C4.2#q05, C4.2#q07, C4.2#q13, C4.2#q18, C4.2#q21. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ecosystem
items.clue: A community of organisms together with the abiotic environment with which they interact.

items.label: Scientific law
items.clue: A generalized principle, or rule of thumb, formulated to describe a pattern observed in nature.

items.label: Detritus feeder
items.clue: A heterotroph such as an earthworm or woodlouse that ingests dead organic matter and digests it internally.

items.label: Combustion
items.clue: The rapid oxidation of carbon compounds in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and heat.

questions.stem: Why is the growth of a population exponential in its initial phase?

options.text: Each individual reproduces faster and faster as the phase continues.
Individuals reach maturity sooner than they will later at higher density.
Growth continues at full speed until the food has been entirely used up.
Resources are plentiful, so most individuals survive to reproduce.

questions.explanation: With abundant resources and negligible competition, predation and disease, natality exceeds mortality by a roughly constant proportion. Each generation adds to the number of reproducing individuals, so the population increases by a constant factor per unit time.

questions.stem: Why does competition occur between members of the same population?

options.text: It does not occur: members of one species share their resources, and competition arises only between different species.
It occurs only when two individuals confront each other over the same item of food, the same mate or the same nesting site.
Individuals of one species have identical needs, so when a resource is scarce what one uses leaves less for others.
It occurs only in solitary species, because individuals living together in a group are by definition cooperating.

questions.stem: Which description of a community is correct?

options.text: All the populations of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria that live and interact in an area.
All the populations of plants and animals, but not microorganisms, that live in an area.
All the organisms in an area together with the soil, water and climate they depend on.
All the individuals of one species that live, interact and breed together in an area.

questions.stem: A tick attaches to a deer and feeds on its blood for several days before dropping off. Which category of interspecific relationship is this?

options.text: Predation, because the tick is an animal feeding on the body of another animal.
Parasitism, because the tick takes nutrition from a living host without killing it.
Pathogenicity, because the tick is a small organism that harms a much larger one.
Mutualism, because the deer provides the tick with the food that it needs to survive.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the exchange between an orchid and its mycorrhizal fungus?

options.text: The fungus supplies mineral ions and, to the seedling, carbon compounds; the photosynthesizing orchid supplies sugars.
The fungus fixes nitrogen gas into ammonia for the orchid; the orchid supplies the fungus with sugars made in photosynthesis.
The fungus takes sugars from the orchid's roots and the orchid gains nothing in return, so the fungus is really a parasite.
The fungus supplies the orchid with mineral ions and water but receives nothing in return from the orchid.

questions.stem: Very few plants grow beneath a black walnut tree, and bacteria fail to grow close to a colony of Penicillium mould on a piece of bread. Which option correctly names the two processes?

options.text: Defence against herbivores by the walnut; antibiotic secretion by the mould.
Allelopathy by the walnut; treatment of the bread's bacterial disease by the mould.
Pathogenicity by the walnut towards plants; pathogenicity by the mould towards bacteria.
Allelopathy by the walnut tree; secretion of an antibiotic by the mould.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes an ecosystem as a system?

options.text: It is an open system: energy enters and leaves it and so does matter, such as water, gases and organisms.
It is a closed system: light energy enters and heat leaves, but all of its matter is recycled within it.
It is a closed system: neither energy nor matter can cross its boundary once the community is established.
It is an open system for matter only, because the energy in it is recycled from decomposers back to producers.

questions.stem: In a local hedgerow, caterpillars and aphids both feed on hawthorn leaves. Blue tits eat caterpillars, ladybirds eat aphids, and sparrowhawks eat blue tits. Which is a correctly constructed food chain from this community?

options.text: sparrowhawk → blue tit → caterpillar → hawthorn
hawthorn leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk
hawthorn → caterpillar → aphid → ladybird → sparrowhawk
soil fungi → hawthorn → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk

questions.stem: What is the source of energy for decomposers such as soil fungi and bacteria?

options.text: Simple inorganic substances in the soil, from which decomposers synthesize their own carbon compounds using energy from sunlight.
Dead whole organisms and dead parts of organisms only, because faeces are waste from which all of the energy has been removed.
The bodies of tertiary consumers only, because decomposers are the final link in a food chain and feed on the top level.
Carbon compounds in organic matter from dead organisms, including faeces, dead parts of organisms and dead whole organisms.

questions.stem: Which organisms release energy by the oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration?

options.text: Heterotrophs at all times, but autotrophs only at night, when they cannot obtain energy from photosynthesis.
All autotrophs and all heterotrophs, in every living cell, throughout the day and the night.
Only organisms with lungs or gills, because respiration depends on breathing to take in oxygen from the air or water.
Heterotrophs and chemoautotrophs only, because photoautotrophs use light rather than oxidation as their energy source.

questions.stem: Why do plants, as well as animals, lose heat to their environment?

options.text: They do not: heat is produced only by warm-blooded animals; plants merely lose heat that they absorbed from sunlight.
Plants respire only at night, so the heat they lose is produced in darkness and simply builds up until the next day.
Cell respiration in every organism converts some chemical energy to heat, both when ATP is produced and when ATP is used.
Heat is released only when ATP is used in the cell, because the production of ATP in respiration transfers energy with no loss.

questions.stem: Which are the correct units for primary production?

options.text: Grams of carbon per square metre of land
Grams of carbon per square metre per year
Kilojoules per square metre per year
Grams of carbon per individual per year

questions.explanation: Primary production is the accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs. It is a rate, so the units are mass of carbon per unit area per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹.
